questiontext.text:
Section 1: Review of Lessons 1–5

Cumulative Review

Lesson 6 builds directly on Lesson 5. You should now be comfortable with the Aphel stem (causative). This lesson introduces its close sibling: the Paael, the intensive/factitive stem.

  • Lesson 5 review: The Aphel stem: ʾa- prefix, causative meaning (‘to cause X’). Perfect paradigm (ʾallep), participle (maʾlep). Comparison with Hebrew Hiphil and Arabic Form IV.

  • Lessons 1–4 recap: Estrangela alphabet; noun states, pronouns and verbless clauses; the Peal participle with enclitics (present); the Peal perfect (past); pronominal suffixes and ʾit l- (“to have”).

5-Question Warm-Up Drill

Answer these questions before proceeding. Answers in Section 8.

  1. Give the Aphel perfect 3 m.sg. of the root q-r-b (draw near) and translate it.

  2. ܡܐܠܦ — what form is this? What is its root and stem?

  3. Translate: ܪܘܚܐ ܐܓܠܝ ܫܪܪܐ (Rūḥā ʾaglī šrārā)

  4. What is the Hebrew Hiphil equivalent of the Syriac Aphel? Give one example.

  5. Give the Aphel participle (all four forms) of root ʾ-l-p (teach).
Warm-up 1. What is the Aphel perfect 3 m.sg. of q-r-b (draw near)?

feedback.text: The doubled middle letter marks the Paael.

feedback.text: Correct: the m- prefix marks a derived-stem participle.

name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 6 · Section 2: The Paael Stem

questiontext.text:
Section 2: The Paael Stem

Core Meaning: Intensive and Factitive

The Paael stem (also spelled Pael or Pāʿel) expresses two related types of intensified meaning:

  • Intensive: Repeated, thoroughgoing, or heightened action. ‘He wrote’ (Peal) → ‘he wrote carefully/copied out’ (Paael).

  • Factitive: Causing someone or something to enter into a state. ‘Be holy’ (Peal) → ‘make holy/sanctify’ (Paael). The Paael turns intransitive verbs into transitive ones.

Formation: Gemination of the Middle Root Letter

The defining feature of the Paael is the doubling (gemination) of the middle root consonant (R2). This is written with a dageš-like diacritic in pointing, or simply by writing the letter twice in some scripts.

  • Perfect: CaR₁R₂R₂eR₃ pattern — e.g., barrek (from b-r-k), qaddaš (from q-d-š), yallep (from y-l-p)

  • Participle: mCaR₁R₂R₂eR₃ pattern (m- prefix) — e.g., mbarrek, mqaddeš, myallep

Cross-Linguistic Comparison

  • Hebrew Piel: The direct cognate of the Syriac Paael. Also formed by doubling R2. Compare: kipper (Piel, ‘atone/cover’ — from k-p-r), bērak (Piel, ‘bless’ — from b-r-k), qiddēš (Piel, ‘sanctify’). The structural identity is near-perfect.

  • Arabic Form II: Formed by doubling R2 (qaddama, ‘to present/offer’; ʿallama, ‘to teach/instruct’; qaddasa, ‘to sanctify’). Arabic Form II corresponds precisely to Syriac Paael in both form and function.

  • Greek: No direct morphological equivalent. Intensives expressed via prefix verbs (e.g., κατα- compounds), aspect (perfect), or adverbs. Latin uses intensifying prefixes or separate lexical items.

Paael Examples: Peal → Paael

Peal (Syr) Root Peal Meaning Paael (Syr) Paael Translit Paael Meaning
ܒܪܟ b-r-k ’kneel, ܒܪܟ barre bless (Peal)’ k ’bless/prono unce blessing’
ܩܕܫ q-d-š ’ be holy ܩܕܫ qadda (Peal)’ š ’sanctify/make holy’
ܝܠܦ y-l-p ’learn ܝܠܦ yalle (Peal)’ p ’teach (ma ke learned)’
ܫܡܫ š-m-š ’serve ܫܡܫ šamme (Peal)’ š ’minister/s erve formally’
ܟܢܫ k-n-š ’gather ܟܢܫ kanne (Peal)’ š ’assemble/col lect’

KEY INSIGHT: When the Paael is applied to an INTRANSITIVE verb (e.g., ‘be holy’), it makes the action TRANSITIVE and FACTITIVE: ‘make X holy / sanctify.’ This is called the factitive use, and it is the Paael’s most theologically important function. Compare Hebrew Piel kipper (‘atone’), qiddēš (‘sanctify’), bērak (‘bless’).

Comparison of the Three Major Stems

Syriac Peal (basic) Paael (intensive/factitive) Aphel (causative)
q-d-š qadaš (‘be holy’) qaddaš (‘sanctify/make holy’) —
b-r-k berak (‘kneel’) barrek (‘bless intensively’) —
k-t-b katab (‘write’) katteb (‘write carefully/copy’) (’ ʾakteb dictate/cause to write’)
y-l-p yalep (‘learn’) yallep (‘teach — make ʾal learned’) lep (‘cause to learn’)
š-m-š šemaš (‘serve’) šammeš (‘minister formally’) —
What is the basic meaning shift of the Paael stem?

feedback.text: The passive of the Paael is the Ethpaael.

questiontext.text: How is the Paael formed?

answer.text: By doubling the middle root letter (qaddaš)

feedback.text: That is the Peal participle pattern.

questiontext.text:
Section 3: Paael Perfect Paradigm

Root: b-r-k | Stem: Paael | Meaning: ‘to bless’

ܦܐܥܠ Perfect — Full Conjugation (Root b-r-k)

Person Estrangela Transliteration Translation
3 m.sg. ܒܪܟ *barrek * he bl essed
3 f.sg. ܒܪܟܬ *barreka t* she b lessed
2 m.sg. ܒܪܟܬ *barrek t* you (m.sg .) blessed
2 f.sg. ܒܪܟܬܝ *barrekt i* you (f.sg .) blessed
1 c.sg. ܒܪܟܬ *barreki t* I bl essed
3 m.pl. ܒܪܟܘ *barrek ū* they (m. ) blessed
3 f.pl. ܒܪܟܝ *barrek ī* they (f. ) blessed
2 m.pl. ܒܪܟܬܘܢ *barrekit ūn* you (m.pl .) blessed
2 f.pl. ܒܪܟܬܝܢ *barrekit in* you (f.pl .) blessed
1 c.pl. ܒܪܟܢ *barreki n* we bl essed

Formation Notes

  • Root: b-r-k. In the Paael, R2 (resh, r) is geminated: b-rr-k → barrek

  • Perfect vowel pattern: a under R1, doubled R2, e vowel between R2 and R3 (same as Peal CeCC but with geminate R2)

  • Suffix set: Essentially identical to Peal and Aphel perfect suffixes

  • Guttural roots: When R2 is a guttural (Ayin, Ḥet, He, Alaph), gemination may be ‘virtual’ — compensatory lengthening of the preceding vowel occurs instead

Comparison: Hebrew Piel Perfect

The Hebrew Piel perfect is structurally near-identical to the Syriac Paael perfect. Compare:

Person Hebrew (Piel) Transliteration Translation
3 m.sg. בֵּרַךְ bērāḵ he blessed (Piel b-r-k)
3 f.sg. בֵּרְכָה bērĕḵāh she blessed
1 c.sg. בֵּרַכְתִּי bēraḵtī I blessed
3 m.pl. בֵּרְכוּ bērĕḵū they blessed

name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 6 · Section 4: Paael Participle Paradigm

questiontext.text:
Section 4: Paael Participle Paradigm

Root: b-r-k | Stem: Paael | Meaning: ‘one who blesses’

The Paael active participle takes the same m- prefix as all derived-stem participles. The gemination of R2 is preserved throughout.

Form Estrangela Transliteration Translation
m.sg. ܡܒܪܟ *mbarre k* blessing (m.sg.)
f.sg. ܡܒܪܟܐ *mbarrk ā* blessing (f.sg.)
m.pl. ܡܒܪܟܝܢ *mbarrkī n* blessing (m.pl.)
f.pl. ܡܒܪܟܢ *mbarrkā n* blessing (f.pl.)

Formation Notes

  • Prefix: m- (identical to Aphel participle prefix)

  • Vowel pattern: m + a + R1R2R2 + e + R3 (preserves gemination of R2)

  • Suffixes: Standard participle endings: m.sg. (unmarked), f.sg. (-ā), m.pl. (-īn), f.pl. (-ān)

Comparison with Hebrew and Arabic

Hebrew Piel participle: prefix מְ (mĕ-) + doubled R2. E.g., mĕbārēk (blessing, from b-r-k Piel), mĕqaddēš (sanctifying, from q-d-š Piel). Structurally identical to Syriac Paael participle.

Arabic Form II active participle: pattern muCaCCiC (mu + R1 + a + R2R2 + i + R3). E.g., muʿallim (teacher, from ʿ-l-m Form II), muqaddis (sanctifier, from q-d-s Form II). The m- prefix and gemination are pan-Semitic features.
What does ܡܒܪܟ (mbarrek) mean?

feedback.text: Correct: m- prefix plus doubled middle letter.

questiontext.text:
Section 6: The Story — Part 6

Yukhannan Blesses the People and Angers the Priests

Narrative note: This passage is rich in Paael forms (barrek, ṣallī, šabbeḥ, yallep, qaddaš, šammeš). It also introduces the central conflict of the Acts: Yukhannan’s ministry challenges the established religious order. Notice the theological contrast between sacrifice (qūrbānā) and faith (haymānūttā).

Key Paael forms: barrek (blessed), ṣallī (prayed), šabbeḥ (praised), yallep (taught), qaddaš (sanctified), šammeš (minister), šabbeḥ (praised again at end). Note also metqaddeš — the Ethpaael (passive of Paael), previewing Lesson 7.

Sentence 1

ܘܝܘܚܢܢ ܩܡ ܥܠ ܡܕܒܚܐ ܘܒܪܟ ܠܥܡܐ

w-Yukhannan qam ʿal madbḥā w-barrek l-ʿammā

w- (and-) Yukhannan (John) qam (stood) ʿal (upon) madbḥā (the-altar) w-barrek (and-blessed) l-ʿammā (the-people)

→ And Yukhannan stood at the altar and blessed the people.

Sentence 2

ܘܨܠܝ ܒܐܕܢܐ ܪܡܐ ܘܫܒܚ ܠܐܠܗܐ

w-ṣallī b-ʾednā rāmā w-šabbeḥ l-Alāhā

w-ṣallī (and-prayed) b-ʾednā (with-voice) rāmā (loud) w-šabbeḥ (and-praised) l-Alāhā (God)

→ He prayed with a loud voice and praised God.

Sentence 3

ܘܝܠܦ ܠܗܘܢ ܐܘܪܚܐ ܚܕܬܐ ܕܨܠܘܬܐ

w-yallep lhūn ʾūrḥā ḥattā d-ṣlūttā

w-yallep (and-taught) lhūn (them) ʾūrḥā (the-way) ḥattā (new) d-ṣlūttā (of-prayer)

→ He taught them the new way of prayer.

Sentence 4

ܘܐܡܪ ܠܐ ܡܕܒܚܐ ܕܟܗܢܘܬܐ ܗܘ ܕܩܕܫ ܐܢܫ

w-ʾemar: lā madbḥā d-kahnūttā hū d-qaddaš ʾenāš

w-ʾemar (and-said) lā (not) madbḥā (the-altar) d-kahnūttā (of-the-priesthood) hū (it-is) d-qaddaš (that-sanctifies) ʾenāš (a-person)

→ ‘It is not the altar of the priesthood that sanctifies a person.’

Sentence 5

ܐܠܐ ܡܪܝܐ ܗܘ ܕܩܕܫ ܠܟܘܢ ܒܪܘܚܗ

ʾellā Māryā hū d-qaddaš lḵūn b-rūḥeh

ʾellā (but/rather) Māryā (the-Lord) hū (he-is) d-qaddaš (who-sanctifies) lḵūn (you(pl.)) b-rūḥeh (by-his-Spirit)

→ ‘Rather, it is the Lord who sanctifies you by his Spirit.’

Sentence 6

ܫܡܥܘ ܕܝܢ ܟܗܢܐ ܡܠܘܗܝ ܘܐܬܪܓܙܘ ܥܠܘܗܝ

šmeʿū dēn kāhnē mellāw-hy w-ʾetragzū ʿlāw-hy

šmeʿū (heard) dēn (but/now) kāhnē (the-priests) mellāw-hy (his-words) w-ʾetragzū (and-were-angered) ʿlāw-hy (against-him)

→ But the priests heard his words and were angered against him.

Sentence 7

ܘܐܡܪܘ ܡܢ ܝܗܒ ܠܟ ܫܘܠܛܢܐ ܕܫܡܫ ܒܗܝܟܠܐ

w-ʾemrū: man yahab lāḵ šulṭānā d-šammeš b-hayklā?

w-ʾemrū (and-they-said) man (who) yahab (gave) lāḵ (to-you) šulṭānā (authority) d-šammeš (to-minister) b-hayklā (in-the-temple)

→ ‘Who gave you authority to minister in the temple?’

Sentence 8

ܥܢܐ ܝܘܚܢܢ ܘܐܡܪ ܐܠܗܐ ܫܕܪܢܝ ܕܐܩܕܫ ܠܥܡܗ

ʿnā Yukhannan w-ʾemar: Alāhā šedarnī d-ʾqaddeš l-ʿammeh

ʿnā (answered) Yukhannan (Yukhannan) w-ʾemar (and-said) Alāhā (God) šedarnī (sent-me) d-ʾqaddeš (to-sanctify) l-ʿammeh (his-people)

→ Yukhannan answered: ‘God sent me to sanctify his people.’

Sentence 9

ܠܐ ܒܩܘܪܒܢܐ ܐܠܐ ܒܗܝܡܢܘܬܐ ܡܬܩܕܫ ܐܢܫ

lā b-qūrbānā ʾellā b-haymānūttā metqaddeš ʾenāš

lā (not) b-qūrbānā (by-sacrifice) ʾellā (but) b-haymānūttā (by-faith) metqaddeš (is-sanctified) ʾenāš (a-person)

→ ‘A person is not sanctified by sacrifice but by faith.’

Sentence 10

ܘܪܓܙ ܪܒ ܟܗܢܐ ܘܦܩܕ ܕܢܦܩܘܢ ܠܗ ܡܢ ܗܝܟܠܐ

w-regaz rab kāhnē w-pqad d-nuppqūn leh men hayklā

w-regaz (and-was-enraged) rab (chief) kāhnē (of-priests) w-pqad (and-commanded) d-nuppqūn (that-they-expel) leh (him) men (from) hayklā (the-temple)

→ And the chief priest was enraged and commanded that they expel him from the temple.

Sentence 11

ܝܘܚܢܢ ܕܝܢ ܠܐ ܕܚܠ ܐܠܐ ܫܒܚ ܠܐܠܗܐ ܒܟܠܗ ܠܒܗ

Yukhannan dēn lā dḥel ʾellā šabbeḥ l-Alāhā b-kulleh lebbeh

Yukhannan (Yukhannan) dēn (but/however) lā (not) dḥel (feared) ʾellā (but) šabbeḥ (praised) l-Alāhā (God) b-kulleh (with-all) lebbeh (his-heart)

→ But Yukhannan was not afraid; rather he praised God with all his heart.
In the story, what does Yukhannan do at the altar?

answer.text: He blessed, prayed, praised and taught (barrek, ṣallī, šabbeḥ, yallep).
He offered a sacrifice and anointed the priest.

feedback.text: He contrasts sacrifice with faith; he offers none.

answer.text: He wrote the law and read it aloud.

questiontext.text: What does Yukhannan teach about the true source of sanctification?

answer.text: Not the altar but the Lord, by his Spirit, sanctifies; a person is sanctified by faith, not sacrifice.
The altar of the priesthood sanctifies a person.
Prayer in the temple sanctifies a person.

questiontext.text: How do the priests react, and why?

answer.text: They are angered (ʾetragzū), because he bypasses priestly authority.

feedback.text: They confront him: 'Who gave you authority?'

questiontext.text: What does Yukhannan claim when asked about his authority?

answer.text: Divine commission: 'God sent me (šedarnī) to sanctify his people.'
That the chief priest appointed him.

feedback.text: The chief priest wants him expelled.

questiontext.text: What does Yukhannan do after being threatened with expulsion?

answer.text: He is not afraid and praises God with all his heart.

feedback.text: Correct: fearless devotion over fear of human authority.
Not in this part of the story.

questiontext.text: The form metqaddeš in sentence 9 is an Ethpaael. What does that stem express?

answer.text: The passive of the Paael: 'is sanctified'

Section 9: Grammatical Summary

THE PAAEL STEM — FORMATION RULES

Formation feature Pattern Example (b-r-k)
Root consonant pattern R1 + R2 DOUBLED + R3 b-rr-k
Perfect 3 m.sg. CaR₁R₂R₂eR₃ barrek
Participle m.sg. m + CaR₁R₂R₂eR₃ mbarrek
Participle suffixes -ā, -īn, -ān mbarrkā, mbarrkīn, mbarrkān
Core meaning Intensive or Factitive ‘bless solemnly’; ‘sanctify = make holy’

Meaning Pattern

PEAL (basic) + R2 DOUBLED = PAAEL (intensive/factitive) ‘to X’ → ‘to X thoroughly’ or ‘to make X happen / cause X state’ q-d-š: be holy → qaddaš: sanctify | b-r-k: bless → barrek: bless solemnly | y-l-p: learn → yallep: teach

Three-Stem Comparison Table

Stem Meaning Type Perfect 3 m.sg. Participle m.sg. Translation
Peal Basic katab kāteb ‘he wrote’ / ‘writing’
Paael Intensive/Factitive barrek mbarrek ‘he blessed’ / ‘blessing’
Aphel Causative ʾallep maʾlep ‘he taught’ / ‘teaching’

Semitic Language Family Comparison

Syriac Peal Paael Aphel
Meaning Basic Intensive/Factitive Causative
Hebrew (cognate) Qal Piel Hiphil
Arabic (cognate) Form I Form II Form IV
Formation key Basic vowels R2 DOUBLED ʾa- prefix

FINAL REMINDER: All three stems — Peal, Paael, and Aphel — share the same suffix set for the perfect and the same m- prefix for the active participle. The stems are distinguished by: (1) Peal: basic vowels only; (2) Paael: R2 gemination; (3) Aphel: ʾa- prefix.

LOOKING AHEAD — Lesson 7: The Ethpeel and Ethpaael (reflexive/passive stems). You have already seen metqaddeš in this lesson’s story — that is the Ethpaael passive of qaddaš. Soon you will master the full passive system of Syriac.
